rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Brevity is eloquent when wording is shorter than its usual measure relative to meaning; it displays command of eloquence, and the discussion distinguishes equal wording from compressed wording.
rows.anchor: فالوجيز باللفظ أن يكون اللفظ بالنسبة إلى المعنى أقل من القدر 1 المعهود عادة وسبب حسنه أنه يدل على التمكن

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet described his gift as comprehensive, concise speech, offered here as an example of the virtue of verbal concision.
rows.anchor: ولهذا قال صلى الله عليه وسلم أوتيت جوامع الكلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording may match its meaning in measure; the author cites this verse as an example of that balanced form.
rows.anchor: وقوله ﴿ قتل الإنسان ما أكفره ﴾ 2 وهو كثير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's and the angels' prayers have distinct senses, but the author prefers a shared core meaning: care and glorification.
rows.anchor: فإن الصلاة من الله مغايرة للصلاة من الملائكة والحق أنه من القدر المشترك وهو الاعتناء والتعظيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Though the verse applies prostration to all, its unifying sense is submission or compliance.
rows.anchor: فإن السجود في الكل يجمعه معنى واحد وهو الانقياد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Compressed expression can carry extensive meaning; the author lists commands to accept pardon and the guided people's security as examples.
rows.anchor: والثاني كقوله ﴿ خذ العفو وأمر بالعرف وأعرض عن الجاهلين ﴾ 5 وقوله ﴿ أولئك لهم الأمن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The short phrase that retaliation preserves life conveys much in few words and surpasses the familiar Arab maxim about killing deterring killing.
rows.anchor: وقد أجمع الناس على بلاغته وفصاحته وأبلغ منه قوله تعالى ﴿ ولكم في القصاص حياة ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Arab maxim is variously transmitted as “killing is more deterrent to killing,” with variants changing the consonants or using “more protective”; its rationale is deterrence through assured retaliation.
rows.anchor: وقد نظر لقول العرب القتل أنفى للقتل وهو بنون ثم فاء ويروي بتاء ثم قاف ويروي أوقى

rows.speaker: الحوفي
rows.claim: Al-Hufi reports the maxim as a saying of Ali ibn Abi Talib and calls Ali's formulation highly eloquent.
rows.anchor: وقد حكاه الحوفي في تفسيره عن علي بن أبي طالب وقال قول علي في غاية البلاغة

rows.speaker: صاحب المثل السائر
rows.claim: The author agrees that divine and human speech cannot be compared in a contest of eloquence: miraculous revelation is beyond created speech and human grasp.
rows.anchor: وقد أشار صاحب المثل السائر إلى إنكار ذلك وقال لا نسبة بين كلام الخالق عز وجل وكلام المخلوق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Many seek worldly gain without receiving it; the author explains this by the parallel verse, which makes the outcome depend on God's will.
rows.anchor: ومنه قوله تعالى ﴿ ومن كان يريد حرث الدنيا نؤته منها ﴾ وكثير من الناس يريد ذلك فلا يحصل له

words: تَقْشَعِرُّ مِنْهُ جُلُودُ ٱلَّذِينَ يَخْشَوْنَ رَبَّهُمْ ثُمَّ تَلِينُ جُلُودُهُمْ وَقُلُوبُهُمْ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: There is no contradiction between believers' tranquility at God's remembrance and their trembling when reminded: tranquility comes from settled knowledge and hope, while fear concerns straying and deserved warning.
rows.anchor: لأن الاطمئنان إنما يكون عن ثلج القلب وشرح الصدر بمعرفة التوحيد والعلم

words: تَقْشَعِرُّ مِنْهُ جُلُودُ ٱلَّذِينَ يَخْشَوْنَ رَبَّهُمْ ثُمَّ تَلِينُ جُلُودُهُمْ وَقُلُوبُهُمْ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse itself combines the responses: settled conviction removes doubt, while the skin's shiver registers fear of deviation and punishment before the heart and skin soften to remembrance.
rows.anchor: وقد اجتمعا فى قوله تعالى ﴿ تقشعر منه جلود الذين يخشون ربهم ثم تلين جلودهم وقلوبهم إلى ذكر الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He distinguishes those grounded in knowledge and certainty from people who only outwardly profess Islam for protection, whose profession lacks the knowledge that settles the heart and dispels doubt.
rows.anchor: الذي يعرض إن كان كلامهم فيمن أظهر الإسلام تعوذا فجعل لهم حكمة دون العلم الموجب لثلج الصدور وانتفاء الشك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The believers' saying “Our Lord is God” is no legitimate ground for expelling them from their homes.
rows.anchor: فقولهم ﴿ ربنا الله ﴾ ليس بحق يوجب اخراجهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exception for those with physical harm is disconnected: a person kept from jihad by harm may intend it, but reward follows deeds, and bodily striving differs from inward intention alone.
rows.anchor: وانما كان منقطعا لان القاعد عن ضرر وان كانت له نية الجهاد ليس مستويا في الاجر مع المجاهد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exception of Jonah's people is disconnected (“but the people of Jonah”); a connected reading would wrongly imply that God asks everyone except them to believe.
rows.anchor: فدل على إن المعنى لكن قوم يونس

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj allows a connected exception by construing “if only” as negation, yielding “no town believed and benefited except Jonah's people.”
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج يمكن اتصاله لان قوله ﴿ فلولا ﴾ في المعنى نفي

rows.speaker: الآمدي
rows.claim: Al-Amidi rejects al-Zajjaj's reading: the disconnected exception is eloquent, connected usage is more common, and interpreting by sense is not an analogical rule.
rows.anchor: وقد رد عليه الآمدي بان جعل إلا متقطعة عما قبلها لغة فصيحة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In “except whom He has mercy,” the exception is disconnected because the person shown mercy is protected, not a member of the class of protectors.
rows.anchor: فان من رحم بمعنى المرحوم ليس من جنس العاصمين وانما هو معصوم فدل على انها بمعنى لكن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A connected alternative is possible if “whom He has mercy” means the one who shows mercy, making that person part of the class of protectors; the author aligns the phrase with the passive reading.
rows.anchor: فان قيل يمكن اتصاله على إن ﴿ من رحم ﴾ بمعنى الراحم أي الذي يرحم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here “except” means “rather,” so the verse says the Qur'an was sent as a reminder, not to cause distress.
rows.anchor: الثاني بمعنى بل كقوله تعالى ﴿ طه ما أنزلنا عليك القرآن لتشقى إلا تذكرة ﴾ 2 أي بل تذكرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In this example, “except” coordinates with the preceding phrase and means “and,” extending the statement to those who wronged.
rows.anchor: الثالث عاطفة بمعنى الواو في التشريك كقوله تعالى ﴿ لئلا يكون للناس عليكم حجة إلا الذين ظلموا ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For “except the one who does wrong,” the majority takes a disconnected exception, while the particle can also function coordinatively as “and.”
rows.anchor: وقوله ﴿ إني لا يخاف لدي المرسلون إلا من ظلم ﴾ 4 أي ومن ظلم تاولها الجمهور على الاستثناء المنقطع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In “if there were gods in them except God,” “except God” is an adjective meaning “other than God,” not an exception.
rows.anchor: الرابع بمعنى غير اذا كانت صفة ويعرب الاسم بعد إلا اعراب غير

rows.speaker: ابن العربي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Arabi says the Throne Verse is greatest because of the greatness of what it entails and concerns.
rows.anchor: قال ابن العربى إنما صارت آية الكرسى أعظم لعظم مقتضاها

rows.speaker: ابن العربي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Arabi says Surat al-Ikhlas surpasses the Throne Verse in two ways: a surah was the form of the Qur'anic challenge, and it expresses tawhid in fifteen letters rather than fifty, displaying divine power.
rows.anchor: إلا أن سورة الإخلاص تفضلها بوجهين أحدهما أنها سورة وهذه آية فالسورة أعظم من الآية

rows.speaker: جد أبي العباس أحمد بن المنير المالكي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Munir's grandfather counts seventeen instances of God's name in the Throne Verse, mostly explicit and some implicit; the hidden agent of “preserving them” is God.
rows.anchor: قال أبو العباس أحمد بن المنير المالكى كان جدى رحمه الله يقول اشتملت آية الكرسى على ما لم يشتمل عليه اسم

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله محمد بن الفضل المرسى
rows.claim: Al-Mursi proposes counting each derived divine name twice, once for the name and once for its necessarily implied pronoun, raising the count to twenty-one.
rows.anchor: وكان الشيخ أبو عبد الله محمد بن الفضل المرسى قد رام الزيادة على هذا العدد

rows.speaker: أبو العباس أحمد بن المنير المالكى
rows.claim: Ibn al-Munir rejects the expanded count: derived attributes cannot independently denote their referent apart from their implied pronoun; al-Mursi accepted this reasoning.
rows.anchor: فأجريت معه وجها لطيفا وهو أن الاسم المشتق لا يحتمل الضمير بعد صيرورته بالتسمية علما

words: وَمَا يَعْلَمُ تَأْوِيلَهُۥٓ إِلَّا ٱللَّهُ وَٱلرَّٰسِخُونَ فِى ٱلْعِلْمِ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author favors joining “those firmly rooted in knowledge” to God's knowledge of interpretation: revelation is meant to benefit people, and it is implausible that the Messenger knew none of it.
rows.anchor: ومنهم من رجح أنها للعطف لأن الله تعالى لم يكلف الخلق بما لا يعلمون وضعف الأول لأن الله لم ينزل شيئا من القرآن إلا لينتفع به عباده

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says he is among the firmly rooted in knowledge and, on the verse about the cave companions, among the few who know their number.
rows.anchor: ألا ترى أن ابن عباس كان يقول أنا من الراسخين في العلم ويقول عند قراءة قوله في أصحاب الكهف

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid reads the firmly rooted as knowing the interpretation while also saying, “We believe in it.”
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد في قوله تعالى ﴿ وما يعلم تأويله إلا الله والراسخون في العلم ﴾ يعلمونه

words: وَٱلرَّٰسِخُونَ فِى ٱلْعِلْمِ يَقُولُونَ ءَامَنَّا بِهِۦ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the firmly rooted knew nothing of the ambiguous verses, their assent would not distinguish them from the ignorant; commentators have consistently interpreted even the disjoint letters.
rows.anchor: ونحن لم نر المفسرين إلى هذه الغاية توقفوا عن شيء من القرآن فقالوا هو متشابه لا يعلمه إلا الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author answers the objection that coordination leaves “they say” without a second verb by treating it as a circumstantial clause, “saying that we believe.”
rows.anchor: قلنا إن ﴿ يقولون ﴾ هنا في معنى الحال كأنه قال ﴿ والراسخون في العلم ﴾ قائلين آمنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another analysis supplies an omitted conjunction, “they know and they say”; the author adds that faith without knowledge is inconceivable and knowledge distinguishes the firmly rooted from the ignorant.
rows.anchor: وقيل المعنى ( يعلمون ويقولون ) فحذف واو العطف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One rhetorical question can combine denial and affirmation: “Which group is more entitled to security?” denies security to the unbelievers and affirms it for believers.
rows.anchor: أي ليس الكفار أمنين والذين آمنوا أحق بالآمن ولما كان أكثر مواقع التقرير دون الإنكار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question about eating a dead brother's flesh can be understood as a report-seeking prompt whose only answer is “no”; Mujahid, al-Farisi, and al-Zamakhshari are cited for this account.
rows.anchor: ولهذا قال مجاهد التقدير لا فانهم لما استفهموا استفهام تقرير بما لا جواب له الا ان يقولوا لا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading takes the question as reproach for wanting to backbite a brother, with “you would hate it” functioning as a command to hate it.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن يكون استفهام إنكار بمعنى التوبيخ على محبتهم لاكل لحم أخيهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further reading treats the question as a denial of their claimed love of eating their brother's flesh: their behavior is attributed to them ironically, and “you would hate it” exposes the false claim.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن يكون استفهام إنكار بمعنى التكذيب أنهم لما كانت حالهم حال من يدعي محبة أكل لحم اخيه

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya sees a literal question in “Have you not known that God is capable of all things?” and reports views that posit an omitted comparison or an independent “or.”
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية ظاهره الاستفهام المحض والمعادل على قول جماعة أم يريدون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects that analysis: the question here is for confirmation and needs no comparison; only a literal question requires an estimated counterpart.
rows.anchor: وما قاله غير ظاهر والاستفهام هنا للتقرير فيستغنى عن المعادل

words: أَفَمَن يَتَّقِى بِوَجْهِهِۦ سُوٓءَ ٱلْعَذَابِ يَوْمَ ٱلْقِيَٰمَةِ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A literal comparison question requires an omitted counterpart: here the comparison is with someone enjoying Paradise.
rows.anchor: اما اذا كان على حقيقته فلا بد من تقدير المعادل كقوله تعالى ﴿ أفمن يتقي بوجهه سوء العذاب يوم القيامة ﴾ 3 أي كمن ينعم في الجنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question about one whose evil deed is made attractive likewise implies comparison with one God guides; the following clause supports the estimate, along with “do not grieve over them.”
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى ﴿ أفمن زين له سوء عمله فرآه حسنا ﴾ 1 أي كمن هذاه الله بدليل قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Knowledge of rhetoric's forms is central to exegesis and eloquence; the author says God's teaching of the Qur'an and human speech alone would suffice to show the honor of eloquence.
rows.anchor: واعلم أن معرفة هذه الصناعة بأوضاعها هى عمدة التفسير المطلع على عجائب كلام الله وهى قاعدة الفصاحة وواسطة عقد البلاغة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author invokes “This is a clear statement for people” and “a clarification of all things” as further scriptural praise of البيان.
rows.anchor: وقال تعالى ﴿ هذا بيان للناس ﴾ وقال تعالى ﴿ تبيانا لكل شيء ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The omitted conjunction in “He taught him clear speech” places teaching speech alongside creating humanity, almost as a substitute, since the human is a living speaker.
rows.anchor: ولحذف الواو فى قوله تعالى ﴿ علمه البيان ﴾ نكتة علمية فإنه جعل تعليم البيان فى وزان خلقه وكالبدل من قوله ﴿ خلق الإنسان ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rhetorical skill strengthens understanding and persuasion, enabling the hearer to accept and submit to what is argued.
rows.anchor: وهى قاعدة الفصاحة وواسطة عقد البلاغة ولو لم يحبب الفصاحة إلا قول الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Eloquent discourse can establish divine doctrines, as the resurrection argument after describing the stages of the human seed makes listeners feel awe and fear of God.
rows.anchor: فمن يقرع سمعه هذا الكلام المعجز استشعر من روعة النفس واقشعرار الجلد ما يمكن خشية الله وعظمته من قبله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Eloquent language also clarifies difficult non-creedal questions; the Prophet's concise reply about resemblance answers a denial of female nocturnal emission by pointing to observed resemblance to the mother.
rows.anchor: وكقوله صلى الله عليه وسلم فمن أين يكون الشبه فانظر كيف أعطى فى هذه الأحرف اليسيرة الحجة على من أنكر احتلام المرأة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Eloquent speech can evoke compassion, aversion, appeasement, anger, courage, or fear, used in praise, blame, complaint, apology, permission, and prohibition; speaker credibility and force enhance it.
rows.anchor: ومنها تمكين الانفعالات النفسانية من النفوس مثل الاستعطاف والإعراض والإرضاء والإغضاب والتشجيع والتخويف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The construction “those who believe and do good—we do not waste” returns from the subject to another beginning, then combines it with the original clause; the implied predicate is that their reward is not lost.
rows.anchor: وهذه الآية تتضمن الرجوع والبقاء والجمع ألا تراه كيف رجع بعد ذكره المبتدأ الذي هو الذين عن ذكر خبره إلى الشروع في كلام آخر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The figure called “demolition” answers a speaker's claim with its opposite, thereby undoing the claim.
rows.anchor: الهدم وهو أن يأتي الغير بكلام يتضمن معنى فتأتي بضده فإنك قد هدمت ما بناه المتكلم الأول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The claims of Jews and Christians to be God's children and beloved are demolished by the replies that God has no child, does not love wrongdoers, and would not punish them if their claim were true.
rows.anchor: وقالت اليهود والنصارى نحن أبناء الله وأحباؤه ﴾ 1 هدمه بقوله ﴿ ما اتخذ الله من ولد ﴾ 2 وبقوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The claim that Ezra or the Messiah is God's son is demolished by calling it only a statement from their mouths and denying that God has a child.
rows.anchor: ومنه ﴿ وقالت اليهود عزير ابن الله وقالت النصارى المسيح ابن الله ﴾ 5 هدمه بقوله ﴿ ذلك قولهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hypocrites' claim that they testify the Messenger is God's messenger is demolished by God's testimony that they are lying about their testimony.
rows.anchor: منه ﴿ إذا جاءك المنافقون قالوا نشهد إنك لرسول الله ﴾ 7 هدمه بقوله ﴿ والله يشهد إن المنافقين لكاذبون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A rhetorical figure called expansion argues from observation of the created order; the author cites the heavens, earth, alternation of night and day, ships, rain, creatures, winds, and clouds as signs for reasoning people.
rows.anchor: منه الاستدلال بالنظر في الملكوت كقوله تعالى ﴿ إن في خلق السماوات والأرض واختلاف الليل والنهار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The stages of the human seed and development are used to make the argument for resurrection take root in people's minds.
rows.anchor: وذلك بعد ذكر النطفة وتقلبها في مراتب الوجود وتطورات الخلقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The depiction of the earth in God's grasp and the heavens folded in His right hand is another example of reasoning about divine doctrine through expansive description.
rows.anchor: وكقوله تعالى ﴿ وما قدروا الله حق قدره والأرض جميعا قبضته يوم القيامة والسماوات مطويات بيمينه

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: One interpretation attributed to Ibn Masud takes “the living from the dead” and its reverse as semen leaving a living man dead, then a living man emerging from dead semen.
rows.anchor: عن ابن مسعود هي النطفة تخرج من الرجل ميتة وهو حي ويخرج الرجل منها حيا وهي ميتة

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya says “bringing out” the man from the seed describes a change of state, as when one says a well-built boy will grow into a strong man.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية في تفسيره هذه الآية إن لفظة الإخراج في تنقل النطفة حتى تكون رجلا إنما هو عبارة عن تغيير الحال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another possible sense is that all animals are dead before God gives them life; the author identifies this as a case of tajrid, or extraction.
rows.anchor: وقد يحتمل قوله ﴿ ومخرج الميت من الحي ﴾ 1 أي الحيوان كله ميتة ثم يحييه قال وهو معنى التجريد

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari reports that Amr ibn Ubayd read “a rose like oil” in the nominative, as though a rose-colored sky emerged from it, and classifies the expression as tajrid.
rows.anchor: وذكر الزمخشري أن عمرو بن عبيد قرأ في قوله تعالى ﴿ فكانت وردة كالدهان ﴾ 2 بالرفع

rows.speaker: ابن جني
rows.claim: Ibn Jinni calls Ali's and Ibn Abbas's reading of “he will inherit me and inherit from Jacob's family” tajrid: the requested heir is himself rhetorically extracted as an inheritor.
rows.anchor: وقرأ على وابن عباس في سورة مريم ﴿ يرثني ويرث من آل يعقوب ﴾ 4 قال ابن جنى هذا هو التجريد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Paronomasia includes exact repetition of letters in different senses, as “the Hour” occurs for the Resurrection and for a period of time; a similar example rebuts the claim that the Qur'an has only one such instance.
rows.anchor: وهو إما بأن تتساوى حروف الكلمتين كقوله تعالى ﴿ ويوم تقوم الساعة يقسم المجرمون ما لبثوا غير ساعة ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second type of paronomasia adds letters in one of the paired words, as “the leg” and “the driving” differ by an addition.
rows.anchor: وأما بزيادة في إحدى الكلمتين كقوله تعالى ﴿ والتفت الساق بالساق إلى ربك يومئذ المساق ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A close-letter paronomasia changes one letter between its paired words; the author groups several Qur'anic pairs under this form.
rows.anchor: وإما لاحق بأن يختلف أحد الحرفين كقوله ﴿ وإنه على ذلك لشهيد وإنه لحب الخير لشديد ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Written paronomasia pairs words that resemble one another in script but differ in sound, as in “they suppose” and “they do well.”
rows.anchor: وإما في الخط وهو أن تشتبها في الخط لا اللفظ كقوله تعالى ﴿ وهم يحسبون أنهم يحسنون صنعا ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the repeated definite noun “the Book,” the first denotes what they wrote themselves, the second the Torah, and the third the class of God's revealed books and speech, following al-Raghib.
rows.anchor: فالكتاب الاول ما كتبوه بايديهم ثم كرره بقوله ﴿ فويل للذين يكتبون الكتاب بأيديهم ﴾ 5 والكتاب الثاني التوراة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A common account says the repeated indefinite “ease” is distinct from the first, whereas the definite “hardship” refers back; some explain the indefinite as generic and the definite as already known.
rows.anchor: والمشهور في تمثيل هذا القسم اليسر في قوله تعالى ﴿ فإن مع العسر يسرا إن مع العسر يسرا ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author concludes that the second sentence emphasizes the first rather than promising two separate eases: explicit repetition implants the point, just as repeating “Zayd has a book” does not imply two books.
rows.anchor: والتحقيق إن الجملة الثانية هنا تاكيد للاولى لتقديرها في النفس وتمكينها من القلب ولانها تكرير صريح لها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The repeated “weakness” denotes different life stages: the first is seed or soil, the next infancy and gestation, and the last old age; the two strengths refer to infant faculties and post-puberty strength.
rows.anchor: فالضعف الاول النطفة أو التراب والثاني الضعف الموجود في الطفل والجنين والثالث في الشيخوخة

rows.speaker: ابن الحاجب
rows.claim: Ibn al-Hajib says repeating “a month” marks the separate duration of the morning and evening journeys; measures of duration are not well expressed by ellipsis.
rows.anchor: قال ابن الحاجب في قوله تعالى ﴿ غدوها شهر ورواحها شهر ﴾ 3 الفائدة في اعادة لفظ شهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The same repetition question appears in legal theory: repeating “Pray two units” may be a second command for a second act or merely emphasis; jurists hold both views.
rows.anchor: واعلم انه ينبغي إن ياتي في هذا القسم الخلاف الاصولي في نحو صل ركعتين صل ركعتين

rows.speaker: الطيبي
rows.claim: Al-Tibi answers the objection that two indefinite occurrences can refer to the same thing by classifying “a god in heaven and a god on earth” as repetition carrying an added point.
rows.anchor: واجاب الطيبي بانه من باب التكرير واناطة امر زائد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The particle “then” can coordinate a detailed statement after a summary, as in creating women and then making them virgins.
rows.anchor: الثامن انها عاطفة للمفصل على المجمل كقوله تعالى ﴿ إنا أنشأناهن إنشاء فجعلناهن أبكارا عربا ﴾

words: ثُمَّ خَلَقْنَا ٱلنُّطْفَةَ عَلَقَةًۭ فَخَلَقْنَا ٱلْعَلَقَةَ مُضْغَةًۭ فَخَلَقْنَا ٱلْمُضْغَةَ عِظَٰمًۭا فَكَسَوْنَا ٱلْعِظَٰمَ لَحْمًۭا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the developmental sequence, “then” can mark an interval; there are intervening stages between the stated transformations.
rows.anchor: وتجىء للمهلة ك ثم كقوله تعالى ﴿ ثم خلقنا النطفة علقة فخلقنا العلقة مضغة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sequence from bringing forth pasture to making it dark stubble also has intervening stages.
rows.anchor: وكقوله ﴿ والذي أخرج المرعى فجعله غثاء أحوى ﴾ 4 فإن بين الإخراج والغثاء وسائط

rows.speaker: ابن مالك
rows.claim: Ibn Malik treats the present-tense result after rain as a consequence, while an alternative analysis supplies omitted stages: the growth comes, then the land becomes green.
rows.anchor: وجعل منه ابن مالك قوله تعالى ﴿ ألم تر أن الله أنزل من السماء ماء فتصبح الأرض مخضرة ﴾

rows.speaker: ابن الحاجب
rows.claim: One account takes the particle as customary sequence rather than immediate succession; years may intervene while the later event still follows the first by ordinary course.
rows.anchor: وقيل بل هي للتعقيب والتعقيب على ما بعد في العادة تعقيبا لا على سبيل المضيافة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another account keeps immediate succession: once the causes of greening are complete, the earth becomes green without a further interval.
rows.anchor: وقيل بل للتعقيب الحقيقي على بابها وذلك لأن أسباب الاخضرار عند زمانها فإذا تكاملت اصبحت مخضرة بغير مهلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The present tense after the particle need not be subjunctive because the preceding question is confirmatory rather than a true question, and seeing rain does not itself cause greening; the rain does.
rows.anchor: وإنما لم ينصب على جواب الاستفهام لوجهين أحدهما انه بمعنى التقرير أي قد رأيت فلا يكون له جواب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Commands following “when” are understood as “when you intend to recite” or “when you intend to pray,” with the cause standing for its result.
rows.anchor: وأما قوله تعالى ﴿ فإذا قرأت القرآن فاستعذ ﴾ 1 ﴿ إذا قمتم إلى الصلاة فاغسلوا ﴾ 2 قالتقدير فإذا أردت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to strike the stone implies the striking action, after which the water gushed forth; this is another case of stating a cause for its result.
rows.anchor: ونظيره ﴿ أن اضرب بعصاك الحجر ﴾ 3 أي فضرب فانفجرت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some grammarians take the two “then” clauses in this verse, including “We clothed the bones,” as having the sense of “then” to mark delayed stages.
rows.anchor: فقيل الفاء في ﴿ فخلقنا العلقة ﴾ وفي ﴿ فكسونا ﴾ بمعنى ثم لتراخي معطوفها
